props.title: Chaplin
props.initialSlug: Robert Downey Jr. as Charlie Chaplin

sections.content: Robert Downey Jr. delivers a tour-de-force performance in Chaplin (1992), Richard Attenborough's ambitious biopic that traces Charlie Chaplin's rise from London poverty to Hollywood legend. The film masterfully weaves between Chaplin's creation of the iconic Little Tramp character and his complex personal life, including his controversial political views and relationships with young women. Like Ed Wood (1994) and The Aviator (2004), it captures both the magic and madness of early Hollywood, showing how Chaplin revolutionized cinema through masterpieces like The Kid (1921) and Modern Times (1936). movies.title: Chaplin
movies.slug: Robert Downey Jr. stars as the legendary Charlie Chaplin in this sweeping biopic covering his rise from Victorian London to Hollywood stardom

sections.content: The film excels at showing Chaplin's creative process and pioneering contributions to cinema. We see him developing his precise physical comedy, innovating with camera techniques, and fighting to maintain creative control through the formation of United Artists with Mary Pickford and Douglas Fairbanks. Like The Artist (2011), Chaplin captures the seismic shift from silent to sound cinema, though Chaplin famously resisted "talkies" with City Lights (1931) and Modern Times (1936), believing pantomime was universal.

What sets Chaplin apart from standard biopics is its unflinching look at the filmmaker's darker sides - his obsession with young women, FBI surveillance due to suspected communist sympathies, and eventual exile from America. The film shares DNA with Mank (2020) in its exploration of how politics and personal demons affected a cinema pioneer. Geraldine Chaplin adds authenticity playing her own grandmother, while the makeup aging Downey Jr. through decades rivals that used in The Curious Case of Benjamin Button (2008). movies.title: City Lights
movies.slug: Chaplin's romantic comedy masterpiece about the Tramp falling in love with a blind flower girl

sections.content: The film's latter half powerfully depicts the personal cost of Chaplin's uncompromising nature. Like Amadeus (1984), it shows how genius often walks hand in hand with tragedy. Chaplin's refusal to adopt American citizenship, coupled with his political outspokenness and scandalous personal life, led to his two-decade exile. Attenborough draws parallels between Chaplin's art and life - both filled with comedy masking deep melancholy. The emotional crescendo comes when an elderly Chaplin returns to America in 1972 to receive an Honorary Academy Award, a scene that rivals the poignancy of the filmmaker's own work.
